newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia-Chechen memorandum seen smoothing oil talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia-Chechen memorandum seen smoothing oil talks.

text.p: Russia signed a memorandum with Chechnya on Friday on transporting oil across the territory of the breakaway region, advancing both a bilateral peace settlement and a major international oil exploration deal.
The route is owned by Russia's oil pipeline monopoly Transneft and runs from the Caspian Sea to Russian export outlets in the Black Sea.

Officials in Moscow and the Chechen capital Grozny, torn by a 21-month conflict between separatists and Russian troops, have wrangled for months over transport fees and how to secure oil moving across the volatile region's territory.
The pipeline is just part of wider talks between the two sides, but is seen as crucial to the republic on Russia's southern rim.
Fighting ended last August but the separatist leaders subsequently elected in Chechnya have yet to hammer out the details of a permanent peace settlement with Moscow.
"It's a practical step forward," said Chechen President Aslan Maskhadov, who signed the deal with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin in the southern Russian resort of Sochi.

The deal is also likely to ease fears among the participants of the international oil consortium, Azerbaijan International Operating Company (AIOC), which has a deal with Transneft to carry its early oil to Novorossiisk in the Black Sea by October.

Details of the terms of the memorandum were not immediately available, Russian and Chechen oil officials said. They said the memorandum was a step forward in relations between the two sides, but did not represent a concrete deal on oil transport.
"There is no final deal as yet (on the question of oil transportation)," said Emir Gantamirov, Moscow-based head of foreign relations for Chechnya's Southern Oil Company, YUNKO.
"It is just memorandum of understanding between the sides. To turn this into concrete action will need further work."
Transneft welcomed the signing, but again stressed that it was not the final agreement.
"Yes, this is an important step," said Ravil Polyanin, Transneft spokesman. "We will get renewed support from the signing of this memorandum," he said.

YUNKO'S Gantamirov said he was confident that the damaged pipeline would be ready before the October deadline. "According to our current work schedule, the pipeline will be ready by the end of August," he said.
Khozhakhmed Yarikhanov, president of Chechnya's Southern Oil Company, said last month that repairs to the pipeline could be finished in 20 to 30 days if $2 million financing was found.

Russian Fuel and Oil Minister Boris Nemtsov said he was confident the money could be raised from Russian private business, adding that a deal on oil transportation across Chechnya was key to the region's economic development.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Maskhadov signed a peace accord last month promising to end 400 years of intermittent conflict between Moscow and the independence-minded north Caucasus region.
Moscow withdrew its last troops early this year after failing to crush the separatists over 21 months of fighting but remains implacably opposed to their demands for independence.

The region has been more or less stable since then, although a wave of kidnappings of Russian journalists has kept tensions between Moscow and Grozny high and talks on the region's future are complicated by the disagreement over its status.

Interfax news agency said on Friday that Russia's customs head Anatoly Kruglov was also present at the Sochi talks, and Chernomyrdin told Russian television that customs -- a sensitive issue -- were part of the memorandum, giving no details.
